Drift, in the context of our course on Large Language Model (LLM) evaluations, refers to a shift in the underlying assumptions or patterns in the data that an LLM is trained on or the way it's used. This can happen due to various reasons, such as changes in user behavior, updates to the platform or system, or even changes in the user demographics, as the instructor mentioned in their example about millennials and Gen Zs using a platform.

The instructor also mentioned that drift can be of many types, including data drift, model drift, and concept drift. Data drift occurs when the underlying distribution of the data changes over time, while model drift happens when the LLM's performance or behavior changes due to updates or changes in the system. Concept drift, on the other hand, refers to a change in the underlying assumptions or patterns in the data that the LLM is trained on.

Drift matters after deployment because it can affect the performance and accuracy of the LLM. If the LLM is not updated to reflect changes in the data or user behavior, it may not be able to provide accurate or relevant results, leading to a decline in its performance. In the instructor's example, if the user behavior changes, such as millennials using the platform, the LLM may not be able to adapt to these changes, leading to a drift in the user's expectations.

To illustrate this, let's consider the scenario where you're taking the last n conversations to perform the evaluation. While this approach may seem straightforward, it's not always effective in capturing changes in the data or user behavior. In fact, the instructor mentioned that it's challenging to come up with a scenario where simply taking the last n conversations would be sufficient to perform the evaluation.

In a controlled environment, such as querying a fixed dataset of 100 documents, the data may not change over time, but even in this setup, drift can still occur due to changes in the user's expectations or behavior. The instructor emphasized that drift has many natures and can be difficult to control in AI-based systems.

When we talk about a benchmark getting saturated, it means that the benchmark is no longer useful for evaluating models because all the models are performing equally well on it. In other words, the benchmark is so easy that all the models are able to achieve a high score, typically above 90-95%.

Let me break it down further. Imagine you're taking an exam, and the questions are so easy that everyone in the class gets an A+. That's basically what's happening with a saturated benchmark. The questions are so straightforward that all the models are able to answer them correctly, and there's no longer a clear distinction between the top-performing models.

In the example you provided, the benchmarks like GSM 8K, MMLU, and SUI Bench are all saturated because all the models are scoring very high, around 94-97%. This means that these benchmarks are no longer effective in evaluating the performance of models, and they need to be replaced with new, more challenging benchmarks.

The life cycle of benchmarks is a natural process, where initially, the benchmark is difficult, and models struggle to perform well. As models improve over time, they start to perform well on the benchmark, and eventually, the benchmark becomes saturated. At this point, the benchmark is retired, and a new, more challenging benchmark is introduced to evaluate the performance of models. This process helps the industry to continually push the boundaries of model performance and innovation.

When we talk about the evolution of benchmarks in knowledge capability, we're essentially looking at how we measure the knowledge retained by a large language model (LLM) after its training process. The flow chart we'll be discussing will help us understand the different components of this capability.

Now, let's dive into the concept of knowledge capability itself. It's a way to gauge how much world knowledge is hidden within an LLM's weights and biases. Think of it like this: when you train an LLM on a massive dataset, you'd expect it to be able to answer a wide range of questions about the internet. That's essentially what knowledge capability is all about – it's the most fundamental capability an LLM can have.

In our discussion, we'll start with MMLU, which is considered the mother of all benchmarks in knowledge capability. This benchmark tests the breadth of knowledge an LLM has, not its depth. While it's true that training on more data can lead to improved knowledge capabilities, it's not a guarantee. In other words, simply throwing more data at an LLM doesn't necessarily make it more knowledgeable. The relationship between data quantity and knowledge capability is more complex than that. In the context of online evaluation, computed and captured signals are two types of signals that you need to focus on. Computed signals are those that you have to calculate or figure out, whereas captured signals are those that are already present and you need to store them somewhere.

Let's break it down further. Computed signals are like the ones you need to calculate to determine the user's sentiment or intent. For instance, if you want to evaluate a user's satisfaction with your chatbot, you might need to calculate the sentiment based on their responses, such as thumbs up or thumbs down. However, in this case, you don't need to calculate anything because the user's sentiment is already present in their responses. This is an example of a captured signal, where you simply store the user's sentiment as it is.

Another example of a captured signal is latency. When evaluating the performance of your chatbot, you might need to store the time it took to respond to a particular question. Again, you don't need to calculate anything here; you just need to store the latency value as it is.

In contrast, computed signals are those that require calculation or processing. For instance, if you want to evaluate the cost per conversation, you might need to calculate the cost based on the number of tokens spent or the amount of money spent. This is an example of a computed signal, where you need to perform calculations to determine the value.

So, to summarize, computed signals are those that require calculation or processing, whereas captured signals are those that are already present and need to be stored as is.
